12957-the-khaki-boys-over-the-top-or-doi:
Captain Gordon Bates wrote The Khaki Boys Over the Top in 1919, fourth in his Khaki Boys series. Jimmy and his mates, already trained at Camp Sterling and tested at the front, go over the top in France, facing machine guns, falling walls, traps, and capture. Chapters move from a blown-back start to a lonely hut and a glorious victory.

A mill assault shows the cost: a lieutenant falls with a dozen bullets in his body, yet the man behind him leaps over the corpse and leads on. Franz, hit only in a finger, shouts that they are with Jimmy still. Bates writes brisk, patriotic boys' war fiction with little doubt and much dash.
14614-sister-teresa:
George Moore's Sister Teresa, first published in 1901 and entirely rewritten in 1909, follows Evelyn, a singer turned nun, through convent poverty and artistic memory. Fisher Unwin published the London edition.

Mother Philippa tells Evelyn the convent has no money at all, and the prioress will not run into debt, leaving vegetables and flour to manage on. Owen later searches for a critic's article praising Evelyn as an artist of the peaks, unsuited to the plain. Moore writes with psychological care about vocation, art, and faith. The novel is a major work of his Irish period.
22458-the-swedish-revolution-under-gusta:
The Swedish Revolution under Gustavus Vasa, dated 1889, tells how Sweden broke from Denmark. The revolution stretched over seven years of rising and war. It began with the uprising of the Dalesmen in 1521.

That rising opened the struggle that freed Swedish rule. It ended with the coronation of Gustavus in 1528. The author claims the period suits two kinds of readers. Students of history will find its politics worth study. Lovers of romance will find its deeds worth savoring. Gustavus Vasa became Sweden's founding king through those years. Readers get his revolution as both record and adventure. It explains a nation's birth through one determined leader.
23856-the-heart-of-arethusa:
Frances Barton Fox published The Heart of Arethusa in Boston in 1918, with a frontispiece by F. W. Read. Fox dedicated it to George Madden Martin, who found her young and ignorant of the writing trade and gave her busy hours to worthier aims. The dedication's verse credits Martin with a part in all Fox has written.

The novel starts where a straight approach lined with water maples in matching rows ends, and its twenty-five chapters follow Arethusa through the world the book builds around her. Small, Maynard and Company published it in the last year of the Great War. It is a romance of its period, written with the earnest feeling Fox's readers expected.
26984-across-the-mesa:
Jarvis Hall's 1922 novel Across the Mesa follows a party traveling the Southwest, from Athens through Juan Pachuca's country to Casa Grande. Polly arrives, a prisoner is taken and set at liberty, and a discovery sends the group on a night ride and a long trail.

Chapters such as Miss Chicago, At Soria's, and Tom Does a Marathon mix humor, danger, and desert scenery. The frontispiece shows a pony putting her forefeet over the edge of a descent. Hall writes a light western adventure, more interested in its people than in gunplay.
278-trinity-site-1945-1995-a-national-hi:
White Sands Missile Range marks fifty years since the first atomic test with this landmark guide. Trinity Site, 1945 to 1995 covers radiation at the site, how to visit, and the Manhattan Project story. Contents run from theory and test-site building to Jumbo and bomb assembly.

The guide quotes Brigadier General Thomas Farrell on light many times brighter than the midday sun. It explains that fenced ground-zero radiation runs low for visitors. Chapters on the Schmidt house, the aftermath, and a reading list follow. The booklet serves visitors and students of the atomic age.
29964-clarissa:
This volume is not Richardson's novel itself, but a scholarly reprint of its framing matter. The Augustan Reprint Society issued it as publication number 103, from the William Andrews Clark Memorial Library at the University of California, Los Angeles, in 1964. R. F. Brissenden of the Australian National University at Canberra wrote the introduction. The general editors were Richard C. Boys, Earl R. Miner, Maximillian E. Novak, and Lawrence Clark Powell.

The reprint gives Samuel Richardson's Clarissa: Preface, Hints of Prefaces, and Postscript, with footnotes to the introduction. Notes cite William Merritt Sale's bibliographical record of Richardson's career, the Hints of Prefaces, and the postscript to the fourth edition. Warburton's preface, as reproduced in Prefaces to Fiction, is also in view. The book suits students of the novel's making, not readers seeking the story itself.
30743-the-philosophy-of-evolution-togeth:
Stephen H. Carpenter, professor of logic at the University of Wisconsin, wrote these two papers for the Wisconsin Academy of Sciences, Arts, and Letters. They were read in February 1873 and February 1874 and reprinted at Madison in 1874. The first paper sets out the metaphysical basis of science, and the second gives the philosophy of evolution. Carpenter writes as a philosopher of science, not as a field naturalist.

His opening claim is that all knowledge is one, and that physics, stripped of what is merely contingent, becomes metaphysics. Physical science, he says, reads the signs by which nature speaks, while metaphysical science seeks the meaning of the message. The papers offer a nineteenth-century attempt to join Darwin's new biology to an older unity of thought, and they still interest readers of philosophy and science history.
3099-the-old-merchant-marine-a-chronicle:
Ralph Paine wrote The Old Merchant Marine, a chronicle of American ships and sailors, for the Chronicles of America series. Chapters run from colonial adventurers in little ships through the privateers of 1776 and the famous days of Salem port. Yankee vikings and new trade routes, free trade and sailors' rights, the brilliant era of 1812, packet ships of the roaring forties, and the stately clipper follow. Paine calls the story an epic of blue water. A shipwreck passage finds Charles Lapham separated from his mates, five days without water.

Rising with effort, he walks toward water two miles away while a companion sympathizes enough to go back with him. The book celebrates American seamanship from sail to steam. It remains a stirring survey of the age of sail.
31109-taxonomic-notes-on-mexican-bats-of:
E. Raymond Hall's 1952 paper sorts out the small Mexican bats of the genus Rhogeëssa from specimens held at the University of Kansas Museum of Natural History. Five skins with skulls came from Sonora and Nayarit in western Mexico, collected by J. R. Alcorn, and two more came from Veracruz in the east, collected by Walter W. Dalquest.

Hall compares these with material in the United States National Museum and reviews the three kinds already named from Mexico. They are parvula from the Tres Marias Islands, tumida from Veracruz, and gracilis from Puebla, of which only three specimens were then known. The note is a careful piece of museum taxonomy, fixing names to specimens so later field workers can tell these look-alike bats apart.
3149-marm-lisa:
Kate Douglas Wiggin centers this story on Marm Lisa, a girl transplanted into new soil. Chapters move from Eden Place and Mistress Mary's garden to a family polygon, then to the transplant itself and how the new plant grows. A line from Goethe's Faust heads the book: the eternal womanly leads us on.

The garden language is the story's key. Lisa, like a cutting set in fresh ground, must root among strangers who mean well and blunder often. Wiggin writes with her usual warmth about children on the edge of respectable life. The 1905 sixth edition testifies to its steady readership among readers who liked their sentiment honest and their endings kind.
31968-the-birth-of-the-war-god-a-poem-by:
Kálidása's Birth of the War-God, the Kumára Sambhava, translated from Sanskrit into English verse by Ralph T. H. Griffith, principal of Benares College, appeared in a second edition at London in 1879 in Trübner's Oriental Series. Griffith notes that little is known with certainty of Kálidása's history, except that he was one of the Nine Precious Stones at King Vikramáditya's court in Oujein.

That court flourished in the half century before the Christian era, about the time Virgil and Horace shed lustre on the reign of Augustus. Readers get a classical Indian poem in Victorian verse, telling how the war god was born, in a translation that made Sanskrit literature accessible to English readers.
33359-the-unveiling-of-lhasa:
Edmund Candler's Unveiling of Lhasa, published in London, tells of the journey to Tibet's forbidden capital, with illustrations and a map. Candler, author of A Vagabond in Asia, writes as a witness to an expedition that opened Lhasa to outside eyes, describing the road, the people, and the city itself. His book belongs to the age of exploration, when a closed land could still be unveiled.

The volume's power lies in its first-hand detail, from high passes to temple streets, told in a journalist's clear prose. Its map and pictures help readers follow a hard road. For students of Tibet and of British India, it remains a vivid, if dated, account of a journey that changed how the world saw Lhasa.
35507-tales-and-trails-of-wakarusa:
Tales and Trails of Wakarusa is a Kansas tale book by Harvey of the Topeka bar. A Crane house of Topeka brought it out in nineteen seventeen. A fore thought opens the book on how past writ is made of noise. Blest are the folk whose years are dull, that old saw starts the theme. Blest are the folk whose years are blank, a wild sage turns it more.

Oak trees grow a thou years in hush ere the axe man comes at last. Rumor chats of what was mis done, not what was done, in that theme. Wars and raids are sin and woe, not work but blocks to work, it holds. Fields stayed green and gold while craft hands and think minds toiled on. Wakarusa tales of that quiet sort ground the scheme of the book.
40216-the-patriarchs-being-meditations-u:
The Patriarchs holds meditations upon Enoch, Noah, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph. Job, the Canticles, heaven, and earth complete the set. Bellett's book was issued in a new edition in London in 1895, by Rouse of Paternoster Square. The opening meditation begins with a disclaimer: the writer's purpose is not so much Enoch himself as the times and the saints before the flood.

The materials, Bellett owns, are very scanty, yet full of meaning in the way and wisdom of the Spirit. He praises the peculiar attraction of Genesis: human life in its infancy and artlessness. Scenes are domestic there, and habits formed by family duties and affections. A great lord's wife kneads the cake for the traveller herself. Bellett writes devotional commentary in the Brethren manner, drawing doctrine and comfort from the plain tales of the first book of Scripture.
40330-inchbracken-the-story-of-a-fama-cl:
Robert Cleland wrote Inchbracken, the story of a fama clamosa, in a new pictured edition. Robert Forrester issued the novel in Glasgow in eighteen hundred eighty seven. The parish of Kilrundle in Scotland forms the scene. Thirty seven chapters trace a storm of talk and shame.

A wild night opens the tale in Glen Effick. Rain lashes the glen and burns swell to torrents. Coach lamps glow like the eyes of a night beast. A find by the stream sets tongues wagging soon after. Names such as Julia, Sophia, and Joseph head the next tales. A child, a charge of false oath, and church court scenes follow. Fama clamosa means a loud ill fame spread by talk. The novel shows how fast such fame can wreck lives.
41929-arethusa:
Arethusa is a tale of Constantinople by Crawford, the Saracinesca author. The Macmillan Company of New York and London issued it in nineteen o seven. Gertrude Demain Hammond drew the pictures for the bazaar storyteller tale. Crawford gives the book to his dear daughter Eleanor on the dedication page.

Plates show Arethusa, an old beggar woman talk, and a tender kiss scene. Rustan calls a negress his Zoe, his life, in one pictured moment. Forty ducats cries Omobono, casting up his eyes to bargain half an hour. Phillips Publishing held the first copyright in nineteen o six and seven. The story teller of the bazaar frames this Constantinople romance throughout.
43101-witty-pieces-by-witty-people-a-col:
Witty Pieces by Witty People is a collection of funny sayings, jokes, and laughable anecdotes. Royal Publishing Company issued it at Philadelphia with copyright in 1894. Many striking and amusing cuts illustrate the joke book for its buyers. Mr and Mrs Bowser opens the fun with a domestic scene at home.

Mr Bowser suddenly looks up from his paper the other evening, the first piece begins. Why have we not given a progressive euchre party this season, he asks his wife. They have been voted too much trouble, she replies in the sketch. Did any one vote besides you, he rejoins in the parlour duel. Newspaper fun, dialect sketches, and clipped jokes fill the pages of such a volume. Parlour and train reading of the 1890s ran heavily to joke collections like this.
43153-donna-teresa:
Donna Teresa is a novel by Frances Peard, published by Macmillan in an edition dated 1899. The story is set in Rome. Its heroine is the young Marchesa di Sant' Eustachio, who prefers to be called Donna Teresa.

The first chapter opens on a sirocco day in Rome. The hot wind brings a damp ooze to the pavement and disposes everyone to peevish views of life. Against the languor, the marchesa and her sister Sylvia Brodrick walk briskly from the Pincio toward Santa Maria Maggiore. The sisters, the narrator says, show little likeness despite what strangers assert. The marchesa is the talker of the pair, eager when in good spirits. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
45061-the-call-of-the-east-a-romance-of-:
Thurlow Fraser wrote The Call of the East, a romance of far Formosa, copyrighted in 1914. A foreword from Owen Sound, Ontario, frames the tale. In every port of the Orient, Fraser writes, the outposts of the restless, aggressive West touch the lines of the impassive East.

Consuls, officers, merchants, and missionaries force western ideas on the reluctant East. Some stay true to high standards; many fall to the level of those they live among, and below it. The story pictures that meeting in one small port during the Franco-Chinese War of 1884 and 1885. One character, Dr MacKay, is called by his own name; the rest are imaginary. Readers get a missionary-era Taiwan romance.
53746-among-the-head-hunters-of-formosa:
Among the Head Hunters of Formosa is an anthropology book by Janet Montgomery McGovern. Fisher Unwin of London issued it first in 1922 with pictures through the text. Marett of Oxford, reader in social anthropology, wrote a preface for the work. A plate shows a man and woman of the Yami tribe in spring festival dress.

McGovern held an Oxford diploma in anthropology and travelled the island at first hand. A quote from Tylor on primitive thought frames her respect for her subjects. Head hunting tribes, rites, and daily life in old Formosa form the matter. The book is dedicated to her son, companion of her wanderings in the field.
55113-from-the-log-of-the-velsa:
Arnold Bennett kept a log of a yacht trip on board the Velsa, with pictures by Rickards and a frontispiece by Bennett himself. The book came out at New York in 1914, and its first part is given to Holland. The yacht enters by the canal from Ghent to Terneuzen in August rain.

Bennett writes of bridges that swing open at once, of clean canals, brick banks, and small ports seen by night. The crew must fall back on a faulty motor when the wind drops. Meals, books, and the snug saloon fill the wet days. The tone is light and amused. Readers who like slow travel writing get a close, day by day view of Dutch waterways from a small British yacht.
58540-certain-delightful-english-towns-w:
W D Howells wrote a travel book on English towns, published in October 1906 with illustrations, opening with a view of Westgate at Southampton. Chapter one lands a pilgrim at Plymouth. Twenty four hours at Exeter follow. A fortnight in Bath takes the longest chapter. A country town and a country house come next.

Afternoons in Wells begin the later chapters, as the contents run on. Howells brought an American novelist's eye to English cathedral towns and market places. The glimpses of pleasant country between towns give the book its subtitle. It belongs to the gentle travel writing Howells produced alongside his fiction and criticism. Harper and Brothers issued it in New York and London.
58623-open-letter-to-president-mckinley-:
Open Letter to President McKinley is a plea by Black folk of Massachusetts. A mass meet at a Boston church took the letter up as its own. The meet sat on October the third in the year eighteen ninety nine. Its head line states the plea is made as citizens, not as beggars.

Archibald Grimke read the letter out as head of the group that penned it. All in the hall gave it their full and joint assent that night. The league of Black folk in the state sent it on to the chief. Lynch mobs and lost vote rights drove such pleas in that hard age. The text stands as a plain claim to the rights of full citizens.
60432-the-real-tsaritsa:
The Real Tsaritsa is a memoir of the last empress of Russia by Lili Dehn. Dehn was a close friend of the Empress Alexandra. Thornton Butterworth published the book in London in April 1922. A portrait of Alexandra forms the frontispiece. Dehn received that portrait at Tsarskoe Selo in 1909.

A poem of farewell opens the volume. It asks what force sustained the empress in days of ruin. Its answer is faith in a God of love. Plates show the imperial family and the royal yacht. Facsimiles print the empress's letters from captivity. The first part is called Old Russia. Dehn begins with her own birth on estates in South Russia.
62527-maria-theresa:
Maria Theresa is a short life of the Austrian empress, translated from the German of W D Von Horn by George P Upton. A C McClurg of Chicago published it in 1905 in the Life Stories for Young People series, with four illustrations. Upton translated the companion life of Queen Louise as well.

His preface sets Maria Theresa among the famous queens of the world. Catharine of Russia, Elizabeth and Victoria of England, and Isabella of Spain keep her company. In statesmanship and patriotism, Upton ranks her with Elizabeth and Catharine. As Catharine improved her empire's laws and frontiers, so the Austrian queen rebuilt her state. The little biography gave American school readers a heroine of the old Europe. Von Horn wrote edifying lives by the dozen in Germany, and Upton carried the best of them across the Atlantic.
65142-barbarossa:
George Upton translated Barbarossa from the German of Franz Kuehn. McClurg at Chicago put out the book in September 1906. It stands in a series of life stories for young people. Four pictures fill it, one of the return of the crusaders. The translator's preface weighs Barbarossa from every point of view.

Frederick the First is more familiarly known by his red beard, it says. As sovereign of the Holy Roman Empire, he stands among the greatest. As a crusade leader he stands among the most gallant. The sketch covers his accession, his campaigns in Italy, and his crown. The disastrous third crusade fills the later part of the book. Richard the Lion-hearted and Philip Augustus march in that company. Two young knights, Raymond and Conrad, become the emperor's charges there. Their father's death on the battlefield brings them to his side.
65299-kalevan-uhri-na-ytelma-4-ssa-na-yt:
Kalevan Uhri, a play in four acts by Eero Eerola, was published by Gummerus at Jyväskylä in 1919. The title means the sacrifice, or victim, of Kaleva. The play is written in Finnish. It was first performed on the stage at Viipuri on April 29, 1919, the first anniversary of the town's capture in the Finnish civil war. Its world is the old tribal Finland of the Kaleva clan.

Karhu, the old chief of the Kaleva tribe, heads the cast, with his wife Ripsa and his daughter Heljä. Kullervo and the wise Marva stand beside them. Their enemy is Semen Ujunoff, a Russian lord of slaves. The first act opens in the great hall of Kaleva. Marva tells a dream of loss: a dead chief carried by youths in white and black, with a coal black horse and a snow white horse beside the bier.
66266-roses-or-a-monograph-of-the-genus-:
Roses, or a Monograph of the Genus Rosa, by H C Andrews, was printed in London by R Taylor and Company and published by the author at Knightsbridge. Andrews wrote the Botanist Repository and Coloured Engravings of Heaths. The book holds colored figures of all the known species and beautiful varieties, drawn from the living plants.

A verse heads the title, hailing the rose as of flowers the blushing queen. In his opening Andrews says the rose, famed for matchless beauty, has been the painter study and the poet theme for ages past. His aim is to arrange as accurately as possible the numerous beautiful varieties with their species. He owns the task is arduous, since roses have suffered neglect and wild mixing. Garden fans get a classic rose monograph.
68201-indian-legends-from-the-land-of-al:
Harriet Rossiter and E C Howard published a set of Indian legends from Alaska at Ketchikan, copyrighted in July 1925. A verse calls the land Al ay ek sa, where red men roamed forests and fished streams. Campfires heard legends a thousand years old, the verse says. An ancient legend opens the book: the Great Spirit raised the waters over all the land.

Waves roared like surf on a rocky shore. A few escaped in canoes and settled where the waters left them. That, the tale says, is why blood relations are scattered so widely. A stranger may enter any lodge bearing his family crest. Raven clan may not marry raven, nor eagle eagle.
68744-the-inquisition-in-the-spanish-dep:
The Inquisition in the Spanish Dependencies extends a famous history. Sicily, Naples, Sardinia, and Milan stand in its title. The Canaries, Mexico, Peru, and New Granada stand there too. The author's other works fill the front pages of the volume. A history of the Inquisition of Spain in four volumes leads them.

A history of the Inquisition of the Middle Ages follows it there. Auricular confession and indulgences take three volumes in the list. Sacerdotal celibacy and the Moriscos of Spain stand in the same roll. Superstition and Force gathers his essays on ordeal and torture. A detailed study of each tribunal was precluded, the preface owns. Such a study is not without its interest, it adds. The dependencies get their tribunals traced colony by colony. The book gives Spain's empire its shadow archive in full.
6888-history-of-the-gatling-gun-detachme:
John Parker, a lieutenant of the Thirteenth Infantry, tells how his Gatling gun detachment served with the Fifth Army Corps at Santiago. He dedicates the volume to the enlisted men whose devotion, courage, and endurance made its success possible. Chapters follow the scheme from its start through the ordnance depot, the voyage, the march, and the camp at Wheeler.

The battle chapters give a plain account of the guns in action, with a tactical study of Santiago and a frank look at the sufferings of the corps. Parker adds chapters on the volunteers, the cause, and the return home, with appendices and an index. The book is both a unit history and a soldier's protest in plain words.
73274-red-mesa:
Warren Miller's Red Mesa, a tale of the Southwest, was published by Appleton at New York in 1923. Miller also wrote The Black Panther of the Navaho. Twelve chapters run from Canon Honanki through The Lure of the Mine, Vasquez, Pinacate, and Red Mesa. The Sun Dance, The Defense of Red Mesa, Gold Versus Nature, and Out of the Desert close the book. The opening shows banded Arizona cliffs, red, ochre, blue, green, and white, scoured by prehistoric waters.

Two riders search the cliff face for a dwelling marked Inaccessible on Doctor Fewkes's map. Big John, a bony cowman, feigns reluctance he does not mean, while Sid, the younger man, insists it is Honanki Ruins or bust. The frontispiece catches Niltci's glimpse of Vasquez with his rifle poised. Miller writes desert adventure with archaeology in it: ruins, mines, and Navaho country.
78946-glimpses-of-japan-and-formosa:
Harry Franck, a famed walker and travel writer, made this book of Japan and Formosa from his own tramp through both lands. The Century Company printed it in 1924, with snap shots taken by Franck himself. A pilgrim of Koya-san, staff and begging bowl in hand, fronts the book.

Franck starts in Hokkaido, the north isle, where Sapporo's main street looks much like an American one. He meets Ainu chiefs, one of whom, he jokes, nearly crowned him with a plow. Plates show Ainu girls, old women with blue marked lips, and rites for a new house at sunset. The book gives a walker's close, lively view of Japan in the early 1920s.
britannica-1911-abscissa: Abscissa is the headword of a short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The entry gives the word, from Latin abscissus, cut off, as a term of the Cartesian system of co-ordinates. It names the distance of a point from the axis of y, measured parallel to the horizontal axis, the axis of x. The word first appears in a Latin work by Stefano degli Angeli, professor of mathematics at Rome, the entry states, sending readers onward to analytical geometry.
britannica-1911-almansa:
A white limestone crag, topped by a Moorish castle, rises over Almansa in eastern Spain. The town sits in Albacete province on the Madrid-Alicante railway, thirty-five miles east-south-east of the capital, amid a fertile, watered plain. Its 1900 population was 11,180, and its name is also spelled Alamanza.

Battle, not trade, made Almansa famous. About a mile south, an obelisk marks the field of 25 April 1707, where French troops led by the duke of Berwick beat allied British, Portuguese, and Spanish forces. Berwick was a son of James II of Great Britain, born outside marriage. Readers seeking the wider war are sent on to the War of the Spanish Succession.
britannica-1911-asa:
Asa was a king of Judah in the old books, kin to Abijah and to Rehoboam. His long reign ran with the reigns of three kings of Israel. Little is told of it past faith change and wars with the first of those kings. That foe built up a town just north of the chief city.

Asa used the last of the shrine funds to bribe the king of Damascus to break his pact and strike Israel. The foe then had to pull back home. Stone from that town went to fort two towns north of the chief city. A tale of a vast win past a south host is also told.
britannica-1911-aversa:
Aversa is a town and episcopal see of Campania in the province of Caserta, north of Naples and linked to it also by electric tramway. Its 1901 population was 23,477. The place holds a special spot in southern Italian history.

Aversa was the first place where the Normans settled in Italy, granted to them in 1027 for help given to Duke Sergius of Naples against Pandulf IV of Capua. The Benedictine abbey of San Lorenzo keeps an 11th-century portal. The town also had a large lunatic asylum, founded by Joachim Murat in 1813.
britannica-1911-barbarossa:
Barbarossa, meaning Redbeard, is the name Christians gave to a family of Turkish sea captains, as explained in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The family held three famed men across two generations. They were Arouj, his brother Khizr, called Khair ed Din, and Khairs son Hassan. A late guess that the name warps an Arabic title is set aside in the entry.

Old Arab records say plainly that Christians gave the name to Khair ed Din. It was no doubt a nickname for the red or tawny beards of the family. Their father Yakub was a coasting trader who settled in Mitylene. He had four sons, two of whom took to sea roving at Rhodes. Arouj was taken prisoner by the Knights of Saint John and ransomed back to the sea. In Tunis the brothers joined as mercenaries and raiders, and seized their chance amid wars of Berber princes.
britannica-1911-bassa:
Bassa was a province of the British protectorate of Northern Nigeria, described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It filled the angle where the Benue river meets the Niger, covered about 7000 square miles, and held an estimated one and a half million people. The province was heavily forested and reckoned one of the richest in the protectorate in natural products. Muslim influence had never penetrated it, and most peoples remained pagan in the language of the time.

Peoples and control take up the rest. The Igbira, or Okpoto, once dominant with a capital at Iddah, had lost ground to the invading Bassas in the west and the Munshis in the east. Britain claimed the districts in 1900 but governed only the western half. A military expedition followed the murder of the British resident in 1903. Courts and taxes then worked peacefully in the west, while the Okpoto and Munshi country stayed turbulent.
britannica-1911-bonheur-rosa:
Rosa Bonheur (1822–1899), born Marie Rosalie Bonheur at Bordeaux, was a French painter of animals loved in England as much as in France. She was the eldest of four children, all artists, and her father taught her to draw. Seeing her rare gift, he let her leave dressmaking, which she hated, and give herself wholly to art.

She showed at the Paris salon from 1840 to 1845 and won prizes five times, then a medal in 1848. Her true fame dates from the exhibition of 1855. From then on English collectors and galleries fought for her animal pictures. The entry goes on through her great market and horse scenes and the honours of her later years at By, near Fontainebleau.
britannica-1911-brusa:
Brusa, or Broussa, the ancient Prusa, is treated in this entry as both a province and its capital city in Asia Minor. The Brusa vilayet, called Khudavendikiar, includes parts of ancient Mysia, Bithynia and Phrygia and stretches south-east from Mudania on the Sea of Marmora toward Afium-Kara-Hissar. It counts among the most important provinces of Asiatic Turkey.

Great mineral and agricultural wealth, many mineral springs, large forests and valuable industries support it. Its exports run to cereals, silk, cotton, opium, tobacco, olive oil, meerschaum and boracite, with two railways crossing the province. Its population is given as 1,600,000, of whom 1,280,000 are Moslems, 317,000 Christians and 3000 Jews. The city itself stretches along the lower slopes of Mysian Olympus above the Nilufer valley. Ravines split it into three quarters. The ancient Prusa stands on a bold rock terrace at its centre, amid mosques and sultans' tombs of great interest.
britannica-1911-canosa:
Canosa is a town of Apulia, Italy, in the province of Bari. Its town entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on the right bank of the Ofanto river, high above the sea. The town was rebuilt in nine sixty three below the Roman city.

Saracens had wrecked the old Roman city in the ninth century wars. The old cathedral of San Sabino was blessed in eleven o one. It has five domes and many ancient columns in its build. A fine throne and pulpit from the late eleventh century stand inside. Next to it stands the tomb house of Bohemund, son of Guiscard.
britannica-1911-colle-di-val-d-elsa: Colle di Val d Elsa is a short place entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It names a town and church seat in Italy, in the province of Siena. The old upper town holds a church from the thirteenth century and fine old palaces. One house there is famed as the birth place of a great church builder of Florence. The lower town holds glass works, and its paper trade dates back to the year thirteen seventy seven. Counts for the town and the wider commune are both given.
britannica-1911-crisa:
Crisa, or Crissa, was one of the oldest cities of Greece, set in Phocis on a spur of Parnassus. Its name appears in the Iliad and in the Homeric Hymns as a strong place with rich land. Its territory ran down to the sea and once held the sanctuary of Pytho. As Delphi grew around that shrine and the port of Cirrha rose on the gulf, Crisa lost ground.

From Cirrha the road to Delphi was commanded, and heavy tolls on pilgrims made its people hated. In 595 before Christ the Amphictyonic Council declared the first Sacred War, took the town, and razed it. Its land was consecrated to the temple at Delphi, and the plunder paid for the Pythian games. Rebuilding at Cirrha in 339 brought a second Sacred War, settled by Philip of Macedon. The ruins still show where the Pleistus ravine meets the plain, near modern Chryso.
britannica-1911-eudocia-macrembolitissa:
Eudocia Macrembolitissa (about 1021-1096) was the wife of the Byzantine emperor Constantine X, as this 1911 Britannica article recounts. She was the daughter of John Macrembolites. On her husband's deathbed she swore not to marry again, and she even jailed and exiled Romanus, who was thought to aim at the throne.

Yet she saw that she could not alone turn back the invasions threatening the eastern frontier of the empire. So she broke her oath, married Romanus, and with his help drove off the danger. The marriage was not happy, for he was warlike and self-willed. When the Turks took him prisoner in 1071, she was forced to yield the throne to her son Michael and retire to a convent, where she died. The article adds that a dictionary of myth once ascribed to her was in fact composed in 1543.
britannica-1911-eusebius-of-emesa:
Eusebius of Emesa was a learned churchman of the Greek church, born at Edessa at the start of the fourth century. He had his first schooling in his home town. He then read church study in two great cities, and the study of the world and of nature at Alexandria.

Two famed church teachers were among his masters, the 1911 Britannica entry says. His name for learning and fine speech grew so high that a great church council sought to set him in the chief see of Alexandria, in the place of a deposed rival. He turned the post down. He took a small see in Phoenicia in its stead. There his skill in sums and the stars led his flock to charge him with dark arts, and he had to flee the town.
britannica-1911-falcao-christovao-de-sou:
Christovão de Sousa Falcão, a Portuguese poet of the fifteen hundreds, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. His family held lands at Portalegre and traced its start to an Englishman. That man came to Portugal in 1386 in the train of Philippa of Lancaster. Christovão's father served the crown on the coast of West Africa and died poor.

Tradition tells of a secret boyhood marriage to a rich young heiress. Her kin broke the match and placed her in a convent, then wed her to another man. The entry says Christovão poured his grief into fine lyrics and an eclogue. It also notes a later doubt: some hold that a friend, not Falcão, wrote that eclogue.
britannica-1911-foussa:
The foussa, or fossa, is the native name of Cryptoprocta ferox, a somewhat cat-like or civet-like mammal peculiar to Madagascar. There it is the largest carnivorous animal on the island. It is about twice the size of a cat, five feet from nose to end of tail, with short, close fur of a nearly uniform pale brown. Little is known of its habits, beyond a few facts gathered by hunters and keepers.

The foussa is nocturnal, and it often attacks and carries off goats, above all kids. It shows great ferocity when wounded, and for that reason the natives much dread it. One example lived in the London zoological gardens for nearly fourteen years. The short entry ends by sending readers to the article on Carnivora for the wider family to which this strange Madagascar hunter belongs.
britannica-1911-ganesa:
Ganesa, also called Ganesh, is a god of Hindu myth treated in a short article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He is shown with the head of an elephant, a sign, it may be, of his shrewd mind. He is the son of Siva and Parvati. He stands for wisdom and sound judgment.

The entry calls him one of the most loved gods of India. Almost every act, sacred or social, in a Hindu life starts with a call on his name. Most books open the same way. His wisdom is of the worldly sort that brings gain in trade. He is thus in a special way the god of the Hindu shopkeeper. He also rules the hosts of heaven who do the will of Indra.
britannica-1911-gerasa:
Gerasa, the modern Jerash, was a city of Palestine and a member of the league called the Decapolis, and this 1911 Britannica entry tells its troubled story. It stands among the mountains of Gilead, about 1,757 feet above the sea. Nothing is known of its founding, though some have taken it for the biblical Ramoth Gilead. From Josephus we learn its later fate.

It was taken by Alexander Jannaeus about 83 before Christ and rebuilt by the Romans about the year 65. The Jews burned it in revenge for a massacre at Caesarea, and a Roman general under Vespasian plundered it again. It was a centre of Greek culture, given to the worship of Artemis, and famed for its teachers.
britannica-1911-gloriosa: Gloriosa is a small group of plants in the lily family. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica places its home in warm parts of Asia and Africa. The plants grow from bulbs. Their thin stems hold themselves up in a strange way. The tips of some leaves stretch into tendrils that grip supports. Blooms sit in the leaf joints near the stem ends. Six slim petals bend back and stand upright. The colour runs rich orange yellow or red. Growers raise them as stove plants under glass.
britannica-1911-gray-asa:
Asa Gray, an American botanist who lived from 1810 to 1888, has a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Paris in Oneida county, New York, on 18 November 1810, he was the son of a farmer. He had no formal education save at the academy and medical school at Fairfield. His first instruction in science came from a professor of chemistry there.

In the spring of 1827 Gray first began to collect and name plants in the field. His formal education ended in February 1831, when he took his medical degree. His first paper on descriptive botany came out in 1835 in print. From then on a steady series of works on plant classification flowed from his pen for fifty three years. His first botany text book, Elements of Botany, came out in 1836, and his college text book followed in 1839.
britannica-1911-gregory-st-of-nyssa:
Gregory of Nyssa (about 331 to about 396), one of the great fathers of the Eastern Church, is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. A later council named him a father of fathers. He was a younger brother of Basil the Great, bishop of Caesarea, and owed most of his schooling to that brother. He entered the church young and held the office of reader for a time.

The article says he felt a pull toward a worldly life as a speaker, but a friend's firm words checked it. In 371 or 372 Basil made him bishop of Nyssa, a small town in Cappadocia. He is said to have parted from his wife, who became a deaconess, though the entry calls the proof thin. His firm stand on the Trinity and the Incarnation, with his strong speech, made him a marked foe of the Arian party.
britannica-1911-halaesa:
Halaesa is a short article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It describes an ancient town on the north coast of Sicily. The town stood east of the modern Castel di Tusa. Archonides, tyrant of Herbita, founded it in 403 B.C.

The entry follows the town into Roman times. Halaesa was the first Sicilian town to surrender to Rome in the First Punic War. In return it won freedom and relief from the tithe. It grew into a place of some weight, chiefly as a port, and passed its mother city. The article also notes a rare find: an inscription there honoring a Roman governor of the republican age. The piece is signed by Thomas Ashby.
britannica-1911-hamasa:
Hamasa is the name of a famed Arabian anthology of poems, set out in a 1911 Britannica entry. Abu Tammam gathered the collection that still bears the name of its first book. That first book sings of firmness and valour in battle and patience in grief. Vengeance, manhood under scorn, and strength of will fill out the title sense.

Ten books make up the whole, with eight hundred and eighty four poems or parts in all. Dirges take the second book and manners the third in the set order. Love, satire, hospitality, praise, and description each hold a book of their own. The entry gives counts per book for readers who want the full map.
britannica-1911-jacob-of-edessa:
Jacob of Edessa, ranked with Barhebraeus as a top scholar among Syriac writers, is covered in a 1911 Britannica article. He was born near Antioch near the year 640. He studied at a famed abbey on the Euphrates and then at Alexandria. On his return he was made bishop of Edessa near 684.

Jacob held the post just three or four years, since clergy fought his strict use of church rules. He burned a copy of the rules in anger and left for abbey life. For years he taught the Psalms and Greek reading of Scripture. He spent nine years fixing the Old Testament text, then died in 708, four months after a recall.
britannica-1911-karamnasa: The Karamnasa is a river of northern India, a feeder of the Ganges on its right bank, which forms the boundary between Bengal and the United Provinces. Its name means destroyer of religious merit, a sense explained by more than one legend. To this day, all high caste Hindus have to be carried across it without being defiled by the touch of its waters. The entry is a few lines only: the river, its boundary role, its ill omened name, and the custom that name still imposes on the faithful.
britannica-1911-lambessa:
Lambessa, the ancient Lambaesa, is a village of Algeria in the department of Constantine, 7 m. S.E. of Batna and 17 m. W. of Timgad. The village, centre of an agricultural colony founded in 1848, is known for its convict establishment, built about 1850. The remains of the Roman town, and above all of the Roman camp, are among the most interesting ruins in northern Africa. They include triumphal arches to Septimius Severus and Commodus, temples, aqueducts and an amphitheatre. Baths and house masonry survive. Cemeteries to the north and east keep their stones in their original lines.

Of the temple of Aesculapius only one column stands, though its façade was entire in the middle of the 19th century. The capitol, dedicated to Jupiter, Juno and Minerva, shows a portico of eight columns. The camp lies about two-thirds of a mile from the centre, its site partly taken by the penitentiary.
britannica-1911-lampedusa:
Lampedusa is a short place article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a small island in the Mediterranean Sea south of Sicily. The island belongs to the province of Girgenti and held 2,276 people in 1901, counting Linosa. It runs about seven miles long and two miles wide, with a highest point of 400 feet. In rock and land form it belongs to Africa, since it sits on the sea shelf off the coast of Tunisia.

Scrub once covered the island, but the cut rock now lies bare and the valleys stay fairly rich. Hut bases, Punic tombs, and Roman buildings near the harbour trace its early life. A thousand slaves were seized from the island in 1553, and in 1843 a lasting colony was planted under Ferdinand the Second of Naples. By 1911 it held a penal colony of some 400 convicts.
britannica-1911-larissa:
Larissa, the most important town of Thessaly, is described in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. It stands in a rich farming district on the right bank of the river Salambria. Volo lies about 35 miles away, linked by rail. Its people numbered 18,001 in 1907, up from 13,610 in 1889. Until 1881 it was the seat of a pasha. It is now the capital of the Greek province.

Long Turkish rule has left little trace of antiquity. The striking sights are the minarets of disused mosques and the Muslim burying grounds. Local making includes leather, cotton, silk, and tobacco. Trade is far from thriving, though Greek merchants moving in have improved it. Fevers are common from bad drainage and river flooding. Many Turkish residents left in 1881 and again in 1898.
britannica-1911-leonardo-of-pisa:
Leonardo of Pisa, called Fibonacci, was an Italian worker in numbers in the 1200s. Little is known of his life. His father held a post at a Pisan trade station abroad. The boy learned his craft at Bugia. Travel round the Mediterranean followed. Back in Italy, he put out his great Liber abaci in 1202.

That book won him a path to the court of Frederick II. A work on land measure came in 1220. At court he solved hard problems set by John of Palermo. Those methods fill the Liber quadratorum of 1225 and the Flos. His grasp of negative roots was sure and early. Luca Pacioli, about 1500, leaned hard on his books. The famed series that bears his name makes each term the sum of the two before it.
britannica-1911-manresa:
Manresa, a town in north east Spain in the province of Barcelona, is covered in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. It stands on the river Cardoner, on the rail line to Lerida. In nineteen hundred it had just over twenty three thousand folk.

The town is the chief place of the high lands drained by two rivers. A stone bridge from Roman times and an iron bridge from eighteen oh four link old and new parts. Its great church is a fine case of Spanish Gothic work. A cave shrine marks where Ignatius de Loyola spent most of fifteen twenty two. There he wrote his work on the life of the soul, the entry says. Iron works and cloth mills give the town its trade.
britannica-1911-maria-theresa:
Maria Theresa was queen of Hungary and Bohemia and wife of the chief ruler Francis, and she lived from seventeen seventeen to seventeen eighty. She was born at Vienna, the first child of the ruler Charles. She wed her cousin Francis in seventeen thirty-six. They had five sons and girls past ten in count.

From her fathers death in seventeen forty she stood at the core of the wars and state craft of Europe. She had a strong bent and a gift for the grand pose. Yet the entry says her charm was true, not feigned. Her plea to the lords of Hungary in a hard hour is told at length.
britannica-1911-massa: Massa, a town of Tuscany, Italy, is the subject of a brief entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is joint capital, with Carrara, of the province of Massa and Carrara, twenty miles south east of Spezia by rail. The entry gives it 10,559 people in the town and 26,118 in the commune in 1901. Its Palazzo Ducale, built in 1701, was a summer home of Elisa Baciocchi, sister of Napoleon. The hills round the town yield marble, shipped from the Marina d'Avenza.
britannica-1911-massinissa:
Massinissa is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Massinissa was king of eastern Numidia who lived from about 238 to 149 years before Christ. He was schooled at Carthage, like many Numidian chiefs. He learned Latin and Greek there. His land was free in name but in fact stood under Carthage and its culture.

The article tells how, as a young man, he drove a rival prince into flight in 212. He then fought in Spain for Carthage with a large horse force. After a great defeat in 206 he cast his lot with Rome. Scipio sought his friendship. With Roman help he crushed his old rival and took his capital. Rome then confirmed him as king and a loyal ally. At the battle of Zama he led horse troops on the Roman right wing. His help was key to the Roman victory there.
britannica-1911-medusa:
Medusa is the name zoologists give to the sea animals known to all as jelly-fishes, as an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica explains. The medusae are sorted by the presence or lack of a velum, a rim of membrane. With their strong muscles and sense organs goes a distinct set of nerves. Where there is no velum the nerves bunch near each sense organ.

Where a velum is present the nerves run as two rings round the rim of the bell. The outer ring is the larger and feeds the tentacles, and the inner ring feeds the velum. A figure in the article marks the stomach, the canals, and the mouth on its stalk. The text notes that body form can vary in all ways that fit this ground plan, from one kind to the next.
britannica-1911-mesa: A mesa, in the study of land forms, is a high table land capped with hard rock. The word comes from Spanish, from a Latin word for a table. Such a form is the remnant of a former plateau. It is common where rock layers lie flat. Hard rock acts as a cap that guards the land below. Valleys wear away faster where the cap is gone. Cases are found in Spain, Africa, Arabia, India, Australia, and North America.
britannica-1911-molesworth-mary-louisa:
Molesworth, Mary Louisa is a life article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a Scottish writer best known for her books for the young. Born in Rotterdam on the twenty-ninth of May 1839, she was a daughter of Major-General Stewart of Strath and was schooled in Great Britain and abroad. In 1861 she married Major Molesworth. Her first novels, from Lover and Husband in 1869 to Cicely in 1874, came out under the pen name Ennis Graham.

Among her books for the young it names Tell Me a Story of 1875, Carrots of 1876, and The Cuckoo Clock of 1877. Those titles, close together at the start of her work for children, mark her turn from grown up novels to the field where her fame rested.
britannica-1911-nagykanizsa: Nagykanizsa is a brief town entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The town stands in Hungary, in the county of Zala, south-west of Budapest by rail. In 1900 it held a little over twenty-three thousand people. It has distilleries and brick works, and trades in grain and cattle. It once ranked as the second fortress of Hungary. The Turks took it in 1600 and held it for ninety years. Austrian and Hungarian forces won it back after a two-year siege. In 1702 its walls were razed.
britannica-1911-odessa:
Odessa, the great Black Sea port, is surveyed in a city entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It ranks with the first ports of Russia in folk and trade. The city stands on a half-round bay at the sea's north-west. Moscow lies over a thousand miles north by the rail lines. Two great rivers, Dnieper and Dniester, drain to its near coast.

Shut mouths make those rivers hard for ships to use well. Trade chose this mid spot from the most old times known. The bay runs deep with a soft floor for anchors to hold. Six harbours line its shore, kept by moles and a break wall. Ice shuts the port for a few days in most winters. A strong ice-breaker cuts that closed time down each cold year.
britannica-1911-orissa:
Orissa, a tract of India in Bengal, is surveyed in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is made up of a British division and twenty four tributary states. Its historic capital is Cuttack, and Puri, with its temple of Jagannath, is world famous. Orissa stands apart from the rest of Bengal in its land revenue system, which rests on a settlement for a term of years.

A new settlement for thirty years was closed in 1900, and it was set to raise the total land revenue by more than half. To guard against floods and famines, a system of canals was built at a cost of near two million pounds. The East Coast railway runs through the province and was opened in full from Calcutta to Madras in 1901. The division holds five districts, with a little over five million people in 1901. The whole of Orissa is holy ground.
britannica-1911-oskaloosa:
Oskaloosa is a city article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Oskaloosa is a city in Iowa, the county seat of Mahaska county. It stands south-east of Des Moines, on a fertile prairie. Its population was 9466 in the census of 1910.

Three railways served the city, along with interurban electric lines. The prairie around it formed one of the state's chief coal-producing regions. The Iowa yearly meeting of the Society of Friends was held at Oskaloosa. Penn College, a Friends' school opened in 1873, had its seat there. So did Iowa Christian College, founded under another name in 1856. A suburb called University Park held yet another school, Central Holiness University. The entry presents a coal-country city with an uncommon share of church colleges.
britannica-1911-packer-asa:
Asa Packer, a coal and rail king, is followed in a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in Connecticut in 1805, he learned the carpenter's trade young. In 1833 he settled at Mauch Chunk in the Lehigh Valley. There he owned a canal boat that hauled coal to Philadelphia. His firm then built boats and locks for the coal company.

Packer urged a steam rail road as a far better coal road. That plan was held too bold for the time by the firm. In 1851 he won control of a rail road stock in the valley. By 1855 a line ran from Mauch Chunk to Easton town. His own credit built much of that line, the entry notes. Spurs to the coal mines and a line north came next.
britannica-1911-park-edwards-amasa:
Edwards Amasa Park, who lived from 1808 to 1900, was an American church scholar. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica traces his life at Andover. He was born in Providence, Rhode Island, in December 1808. His father was a minister and a professor at Brown.

Park studied at Brown and at Andover seminary and taught at Amherst. He then held chairs at Andover for more than forty years. He led the new school of New England theology. For decades he edited a leading church review and shaped its views. His creed statements set out orthodox Congregational belief for his day. A famed sermon of his sparked a long clash with Charles Hodge.
britannica-1911-pianosa:
Pianosa is a flat island of Italy in the province of Leghorn. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica notes its exile and penal past. It forms part of the commune of Marciana on Elba. Its count in 1881 was about seven hundred seventy-four.

As its name says, the island is quite flat throughout. Its highest point stands only ninety-five feet above the sea. The whole island covers about six square miles. Augustus banished his grandson Agrippa Postumus to its shore. Ruins of baths by the harbor still bear that name. Pisa and Genoa fought over it in the middle ages. From 1390 it fell to the prince of Piombino. A Turkish fleet emptied it of people in 1553. Settlers returned only in the early nineteenth century. A penal colony was planted there in 1857.
britannica-1911-shannon-james-jebusa:
James Jebusa Shannon was an artist of both England and America who was born at Auburn in New York in eighteen sixty-two. At age eight his folk took him to Canada. At age sixteen he went to England and learned art at South Kensington. In three years he won the gold prize for figure work.

A face study of a queens maid drew eyes at the chief London show in eighteen eighty-one. A hunt scene six years on won prizes at Paris, Berlin, and Vienna. He soon led the face painters of London. A work of his was bought for the state hall in nineteen one.
britannica-1911-staraya-russa:
Staraya Russa, a town of Russia in the government of Novgorod, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on the river Polista, south of the city of Novgorod, and by that river it is linked by steamer with Saint Petersburg. Its people numbered a little over fifteen thousand.

Brine springs east of the town supplied salt till 1865, and by the time of the entry they served only as mineral waters, much like those of Kreuznach in Germany. Some thousands of visitors came to them each summer. For that reason Staraya Russa was better built and better kept than any other town in its government, and its folk lived chiefly off the summer guests. A trade in rye, oats and flax went out to Saint Petersburg. The town's name appears in Russian annals as far back as 1167, when it belonged to the republic of Novgorod.
britannica-1911-stresa: Stresa is a village of Piedmont, Italy, in the province of Novara. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica places it on the west side of Lago Maggiore. It stands on the Simplon railway, north of Arona, above the lake. Its people numbered 1,477 in 1901 by the count given. Fine villas and fine views of lake scenery mark the place. Guests crowd it in spring, summer, and autumn as a resort.
britannica-1911-tortosa:
Tortosa is a walled city of north east Spain in Tarragona province. Its city entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on the Ebro river, twenty two miles above its mouth. Most of the old town sits on the left bank of the river.

Narrow crooked streets and tall granite houses mark the old town core. An old castle on the slope now serves as barracks and a hospital. The cathedral stands on the site of a Moorish mosque from nine fourteen. Work in the town covers paper, hats, leather, ropes, and soap. A rich fishery works the river, and small ships use the harbour.
britannica-1911-tuscaloosa:
Tuscaloosa is a city of Alabama described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is the county seat of its county and stands on the Black Warrior river, in the west-central part of the state. Two rail lines serve it. Its people grew from 5,094 in 1900 to 8,407 in 1910, and the river by it has been made fit for boats by locks.

The city lies between the foothills of the Appalachians and the low flat of the river. It holds many old-style homes and gardens and a fine federal building. It is the seat of the university of Alabama and of three colleges for women and a school for black ministers. The university was founded by an act of 1820 on a grant of public lands from the United States. It opened in 1831, when the city was the state capital.
britannica-1911-vasa: Vasa, also called Nikolaistad, is a town in Finland noted in a short 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. It is the capital of the province of Vasa. It stands on the east coast of the Gulf of Bothnia, north west of Helsingfors by rail. In nineteen oh four it had just over eighteen thousand folk. Schools include lyceums for boys and girls and a school for sailors. A ship yard and a good export trade are also named.
britannica-1911-walker-francis-amasa:
Francis Amasa Walker, an American soldier and economist who lived from 1840 to 1897, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in Boston, he was the son of Amasa Walker, a noted economist who lectured at Oberlin and Harvard and sat in Congress. His father's chief work, The Science of Wealth, won great use as a textbook.

Francis finished at Amherst College in 1860, read law, and fought in the Northern army through the whole Civil War. He rose from sergeant major to brevet brigadier general of volunteers, a rank given at the request of General Hancock. As a soldier he excelled at reading the foe's position and strength. In 1864 he was captured and held for a time in Libby Prison at Richmond. After the war he wrote for a Springfield newspaper, and in 1869 he was made chief of the government bureau of statistics.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-agostino-barb:
Agostino Barbosa was a noted canonist born at Guimaraens, Portugal, in 1589. He was consecrated at Rome on 22 March 1649 as Bishop of Ugento in Otranto, Italy, and died seven months later. Canon law studies at home preceded his move to Rome. Without books, his astounding memory stood in their stead. Sanctity and affability won him entrance to the city's libraries.

There long hours went to sedulous reading and effortless memorizing, so that back in his room he could write out the day's fruits. About 1632 Madrid took him; there he gave himself to writing and various duties until 1648. Among his many writings are Pastoralis Sollicitudinis on the bishop's office and power, Rome 1621. A similar work on parish priests followed in 1632, plus Variae Juris Tractationes and Juris Ecclesiastici Universi Libri III. All his canonical works were published at Lyons in 1657-75 in 19 volumes, and again in 1698-1716 in 20 volumes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alonso-de-esp:
Alonso de Espinosa was a sixteenth-century Spanish priest and historian. Little survives about his early life. He first appears late in the century in Guatemala, a Dominican. In Central America he heard of Our Lady of Candelaria's miracles. The Virgin and Child image had been among Tenerife's Guanches since long before their conversion, venerated by Guanches and later by Spaniards.

Inspired by its fame, Espinosa found a member of its possessing fraternity and resolved to write its history and miracles. The result, Guanches of Tenerife, appeared at Seville in 1594. Though his purpose was Our Lady of Candelaria's history, the work is the fullest account of the Guanches, a lost race leaving scarcely any remains, even of their language. It also covers the Spanish conquest of the Canary Islands. He divides the work into four books: Tenerife and its inhabitants, the image's history, the Spanish invasion, and the miracles.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-arethusa:
Arethusa was a titular see of Syria near Apameia, with a bishops' list from 325 to 680 in Gams. Briefly it was a Latin see during the Crusades from 1099 to 1100. Under Constantius, who ruled from 337 to 361, its bishop Marcus destroyed a pagan temple, which under Julian he was commanded to rebuild. To avoid the order he fled the city, but returned to save his Christian people from paying the price in his place.

He then suffered very cruel treatment at the hands of a pagan mob, as Sozomen relates. Marcus is said to have authored the Creed of Sirmium of 351, and Tillemont counts him an Arian in belief and factious spirit. The entry joins a small see's long list to one bishop's costly return, showing a pastor who chose suffering over letting his flock pay for his act.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aversa:
Aversa is a diocese comprising twenty-one towns in the province of Caserta and twelve in the province of Naples, under the immediate jurisdiction of the Holy See. The city itself is of fairly recent origin, rising in the eleventh century on the ruins of Atella. Atella belonged to the Oscans, famed for sharp raillery that fed the licentious interludes called Atellanae. Its ruins, left by barbarian invasions, still stand near Arpino.

On those ruins the Norman duke Robert Guiscard built a fortification that grew into the city called Aversa. Guiscard, now a papal vassal backing the pope against the emperor, won leave from Leo IX to move the Bishopric of Atella to Aversa. The city holds many fine monuments in Norman style. It counts 54 parishes, 177 churches, chapels, and oratories, 674 secular clergy, and a population of 130,100.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bartholomew-o:
Bartholomew of Edessa was a Syrian writer who argued for the faith, born, it seems, at Edessa, where he was a monk. His dates are doubtful, but he certainly wrote after Muslims took Syria and the image fight begun in 725. His Greek reply to a Muslim called Agarenus, titled Elenchus et Confutatio Agareni, survives with its beginning lost.

It opens with Muslim pleas against the Trinity, the Incarnation, and Confession, then answers them with counter-charges against Mohammed. Arguing from the prophet's life, Bartholomew finds nothing in his birth, schooling, or life showing a divine call. He concludes that Mohammed preached with no divine proof, and he boasts of having read all the Arabs' books. A second treatise, Contra Muhammedum, is wrongly ascribed to him, differing on wives, the Koran's editor, and his Nestorian teacher.

Bartholomew of Pisa, properly Rinonico, was a Friar Minor and chronicler of noble Pisan family. Long confusion credited his famous Book of Conformities to his namesake Bartholomew Albisi, also of Pisa. A Bologna student in 1352, he later lectured at Bologna, Padua, Pisa, Siena, and Florence, and preached for many years across Italy. He died about 1401, renowned for sanctity and learning, and is commemorated on 4 November.

His chief fame rests on De Conformitate, begun in 1385, matching St Francis's life to Christ's, and approved at Assisi in 1399. Enthusiastically received, it later drew bitter Lutheran and Jansenist attacks, answered by Henry Sedulius in 1607. Later writers ostracized it undeservedly, though recent circles praise it, sometimes to exaggeration. Its Summa Casuum Conscientiae ascription is also wrong: that work belongs to Bartholomew of San Concordio.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-basilissa:
Basilissa is the shared name of various female martyrs from different places, listed in early and medieval martyrologies. Nothing is known positively about any one of them, and their Acts are purely legendary, of later origin. Yet the name's repeat appearances prove that several martyrs called Basilissa were truly venerated in the ancient Church. The same martyr may also stand recorded on different days.

Julian and Basilissa of Antioch appear on 6 January, though legend says she died naturally while Julian was martyred under Diocletian. Other Basilissas appear on 12 March as Felicio's wife in Asia, and on 13 March as a Nicomedian presbyter's wife. The present martyrology keeps Basilissa of Antioch on 9 January, Basilissa and Callinice on 22 March, and Basilissa of Nicomedia on 3 September.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-berissa:
Berissa, a titular see in Asia Minor, is the subject of this brief 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Modern scholars place it at Baulus or Bolus, a village southwest of Tokat in Pontus. In St. Basil's day it lay within the diocese of Ibora, but soon after it became its own bishopric in Armenia Prima, under Sebasteia.

Its bishop Maxentius signed a synodal letter to Emperor Leo before 458, fixing its independent standing by that date. Later lists of sees treat it unevenly, a sign of its small size. The entry is a short geographical detective note on a see that survives mainly in lists.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-agnellus-o:
Blessed Agnellus of Pisa, founder of the English Franciscan province, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Pisa about 1195 to the noble Agnelli family, he died at Oxford in 1236. Received into the order by St. Francis himself during Francis's stay at Pisa, he soon became a model of religious life.

Sent to Paris, he built a convent and served as custos, or guardian. After the Chapter of Mats he sailed for England, landing at Dover with nine friars in September 1224. From that small band grew the English province, with houses at Oxford, London, and beyond. The entry presents a founder working from a handful of brothers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-bernardine:
Blessed Bernardine of Fossa, a Franciscan historian and spiritual writer, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Fossa in 1420 to the noble Amici family, he died at Aquila in 1503, a town so tied to him that he is sometimes called Aquilanus. Law study at Perugia preceded his taking the habit from St. James of the Marches in 1445.

From his entry into religion he never wavered in observance, the entry says, and his chronicle of the Franciscan order preserves early history. Ascetical writings on the spiritual life complete the portrait. The entry presents a steady friar who wrote the order's memory.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bosa:
Bosa, a Sardinian diocese in Cagliari province, counts 40,200 people across 21 parishes with 104 churches and chapels. Gregory the Great mentions a Bishop of Bosa without naming him, and in 1073 Constantino de Castro, who built the cathedral of Saint Peter, became Metropolitan of Torres under Gregory VII. Later bishops include Cardinal Giovanni Casanova, the learned Servite general Serafino Esquirro, and Francesco Fara, author of the first, though very faulty, history of Sardinia.

Some claim the see moved from Calmedia after its ruin. Others say Saint Emilius, sent by Saint Peter, was its first bishop and martyr in 70. No historical proof supports either tale.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-brusa:
Brusa, a titular see of Bithynia, stands in a fertile plain below Mount Olympus. Strabo credits King Prusias with its founding, and the likelier founder is Prusias of Bithynia, Hannibal's friend, who ruled from 237 to 192 before Christ. It became a chief city of Roman Bithynia, took the faith early, and lost at least three bishops, Alexander, Patritius, and Timothy, to persecution.

First subject to Nicomedia, it became an exempt archbishopric by the thirteenth century. Monasteries at Olympus made it, with Athos, a great center of Greek monastic life from the eighth to the fourteenth centuries. Sultan Orkhan took it in 1327 after a ten-year siege, and it stayed the Ottoman capital until 1453. Today its mosques, sultans' tombs, thermal waters, and more than fifty silk mills serve about 80,000 people.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cabasa:
Cabasa was a titular see of Egypt, matched with the village of Shabas, about seven and a half miles north of Sais. It figures in a seventh-century Coptic-Arabic list of bishops under forms like Shabas-Sanhoul, while Ptolemy calls it Kabasa and makes it capital of the fifth district, the Kabasites. Pliny, Georgius Cyprius, and Hierocles also name it.

About 840 a church list gives Cabasa as the metropolis of Egypt Secunda. Known bishops number only two: Theopemptus, at Ephesus in 431 and 449, and Macarius, who opposed Dioscorus at Chalcedon in 451. Its coins also survive as a mark of the old city.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-canossa:
Canossa was Matilda of Tuscany's castle in the Apennine foothills about eighteen miles from Parma. It was the scene of King Henry IV of Germany's dramatic penance before Pope Gregory VII. Excommunicated in February 1076, Henry faced desertion by hostile German princes unless he made peace with the pope within a year.

In January 1077 Gregory, traveling toward a diet at Augsburg, took refuge in the strong castle. He had learned that Henry crossed Mont Cenis. For three days, 25 to 27 January, the king stood at the gate in penitent dress begging forgiveness. Gregory at last restored him to communion and promised to seek his reconciliation with the German princes. Henry soon broke his oath and renewed the conflict.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-capsa:
Capsa was a titular see of North Africa, a town whose founding legend names the Libyan Hercules. It was later held by King Jugurtha, who stored his treasures there. Marius captured and destroyed it in 106 B.C., yet it rose again as a Roman colony. Under Justinian it joined the province of Byzacena. Its duke resided in the strong citadel town then called Justiniana Capsa.

Five bishops are known between 255 and 484, one of them a Donatist. In the eleventh century, following the Arab takeover, the surrounding region held over two hundred thriving villages. The modern town is Gafsa in Tunisia, a fertile oasis town of about 5,000 people. Its people trade in dates, carpets, and wool rugs. The town serves as a center of French military and civil administration.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-colle-di-val-:
Umberto Benigni's entry covers Colle di Val d'Elsa, a Tuscan town on a lofty hill above the River Elsa. It lies in the province of Siena. The town is said to have been built by folk from Gracchiano. They had suffered in the wars between Florence and Siena. Legend holds that Saint Martial, a reputed disciple of Saint Peter, first preached the Gospel there. Its collegiate church stood free of the neighboring bishop's rule. It grew famous through its archpriest Saint Albert, who flourished about 1202.

Clement VIII erected the Diocese of Colle in 1598, at the request of Grand Duke Ferdinand of Tuscany. He named Usimbardo Usimbardi its first bishop. As a suffragan of Florence it counted 72 parishes and 117 churches and chapels. It counted 115 secular and 20 regular priests, plus three religious houses each of men and women.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-council-of-pi:
The Council of Pisa arose after thirty years of Western Schism, when compromise, surrender, and princely force had all failed to end the division. Cardinals of both rival popes, Gregory XII at Rome and Benedict XIII at Avignon, resolved on a council as the stronger remedy. On the feast of the Annunciation, four patriarchs, twenty-two cardinals, and eighty bishops assembled in Pisa cathedral.

Judgment fell on both claimants: deposed from office and dignity, driven from the Church, their acts annulled and the Holy See declared vacant. Cardinals then elected Peter Philarghi as Alexander V, who confirmed the council's ordinances and united the colleges. Theologians and canonists, the entry notes, judge the council severely, since rival popes refused to yield.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-domingos-cald:
Domingos Caldas-Barbosa was a Brazilian poet born at Rio de Janeiro in 1740 of a white father and a black mother. Trained at the Jesuit college there, he won fame for improvising verse, which he turned against the Portuguese whites and thereby stirred them against him. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry tells how his enemies had him drafted into troops bound for Sacramento, where he stayed until 1762.

Back in Rio he sailed for Portugal and won the patronage of the Vasconcellos nobles. Taking minor orders, he became chaplain to the Casa da Supplicacao. Though a mulatto, he entered high Lisbon society, and his songs, gathered as the Viola de Lereno in 1825, kept his academic name Lereno alive. He died at Lisbon in 1800.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edessa:
Edessa was a titular archiepiscopal see in Osrhoene, that part of Mesopotamia famed for its Christian school. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry notes that its cuneiform name is unknown, while its native name was Osroe, after a local satrap, giving Syriac Ourhoi and Arabic Er Roha, now Orfa or Urfa. Seleucus Nicator rebuilt the town in 303 before Christ and named it Edessa for the old Macedonian capital.

Under Antiochus the Fourth, settlers from Antioch renamed it Antiochia. On the founding of the kingdom of Osrhoene, Edessa became its capital under the Abgar dynasty, a realm set up by Nabataean or Arab tribes that lasted nearly four centuries. The entry cites Lavigerie, Ducange, and Cuinet on the city and its monuments.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-elusa:
Elusa was a titular see of Palaestina Tertia, suffragan of Petra, called Chellous in the Greek text of Judith. Ancient writers mention it often: Ptolemy places it in Idumaea, Stephanus Byzantius notes it once lay in Arabia, and Jerome, Theodosius, Antoninus of Piacenza, and John Moschus all name it. In the fourth century a great temple of Aphrodite stood there.

Saint Hilarion seems to have brought Christianity to Elusa, so Jerome's life of him says. Early in the next century a bishop of Elusa ransomed the son of Saint Nilus from Arab captors and ordained both father and son. Other known bishops are Theodulus in 431, Aretas in 451, Peter in 518, and Zenobius in 536. Today its ruins stand at El-Khalasa, about nineteen miles south of Beersheba, in a plain held by nomad tribes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-emesa:
Emesa was a titular see of Phoenicia Secunda, suffragan of Damascus, famed for its temple of the sun. There the sun was worshipped in the shape of a black stone, and its priests formed a powerful aristocracy. One of them, Bassianus, became the Roman emperor Elagabalus in 218. An Arab dynasty ruled the city from 65 before Christ to the year 73, and its coin series dates from that age.

Emesa gave birth to Longinus, the philosopher and friend of Queen Zenobia, and to Saint Romanos, the great Byzantine hymn writer. Among its Greek bishops were Saint Silvanus, martyred about 312, Eusebius the rhetorician, and Nemesius, friend of Basil and Cyril. Raised to an autocephalous archbishopric in 452 and a metropolitan see in 761, it fell to the Arabs in 636, to Crusaders in 1110, and to an earthquake in 1157. The modern city is Homs on the Orontes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fausto-de-elh:
Fausto de Elhuyar was a Spanish mineralogist and chemist of the Spanish Enlightenment. Born in 1755, he taught at the School of Mines in Vergara. With his brother Juan Jose, he first isolated tungsten in 1783. He named the metal Wolfram, still its German name today.

Elhuyar then travelled three years through Central Europe for study. In Mexico he ran the mines and founded a celebrated Royal School of Mines. Driven out by revolution, he returned to Spain and reorganised mining. He died of apoplexy in 1833, leaving many works on silver, coinage, and mining.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francesco-cos:
Francesco Cossa, sometimes called del Cossa, was an Italian painter of the Ferrara school, born about 1430 and dead probably at Ferrara in 1485, noted above all for fresco work. He first appears in 1456 as assistant to his father Cristofano, painting carvings and statues on the high altar of the bishop's palace chapel at Ferrara. With Cosimo Tura he decorated the Schifanoia summer retreat, and three surviving frescoes there can be safely given to him, rich in architecture and period dress.

Feeling underpaid by Duke Borso, Cossa left Ferrara for Bologna in 1470 and won commissions under the Bentivogli. His two masterpieces there are the Virgin and Child with saints and a portrait of Alberto de' Catanei from 1474, and the Madonna del Baracano fresco of 1472. In them he shows stately conception, grand and massive portraiture, broad modelling, and simple, severe composition, stronger and grander, if less decorative, than Tura's work.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-garcia-de-loa:
Garcia de Loaisa, cardinal and archbishop of Seville, rose from a Salamanca novice to the ear of an emperor. Born at Talavera around 1479 to noble parents, he entered the Dominicans young, taught philosophy and theology, and led Saint Gregory's College at Valladolid. In 1518, at the Rome chapter, his order chose him general by unanimous vote, succeeding Cardinal Cajetan.

Back in Spain he became confessor to Charles V, who had him made bishop of Osma in 1524. Clement VII raised him to cardinal in 1530, moved him to Sigüenza, then in 1531 to Seville with the Inquisition's commissary-generalship. His letters to Charles from 1530 to 1532, found at Simancas, light up the Reformation and Spain's politics alike, showing the trust his emperor placed in him.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gerasa:
Gerasa, a titular see in Arabia under Antioch, was a Decapolis city where Jews held power. Josephus tells how Alexander Jannaeus seized it despite its triple wall, and Vespasian sacked it in 68 because Jews ruled there. Simon son of Gioras, rebel leader, was born at Gerasa. It was also called Antioch on the Chrysorrhoas, its little river.

The Gospels' Gerasenes likely mean another place near Lake Tiberias. Gerasa prospered in the first centuries, its buildings dating from second- and third-century emperors, until earthquakes and Arab invasions ruined it. Three Greek bishops are known: Exairesius, Plancus of 451, and Aeneas, builder of Saint Theodore's church. Baldwin II failed to take it in 1121, and by Yakut's day it stood empty. Circassians later settled its ruins and wrecked spared monuments. Yet Djerasch remained the best-preserved Roman city, its arch, theatres, forum of fifty-five columns, and three miles of ramparts standing.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-harpasa:
Caria's Harpasa, a titular see suffragan of Stauropolis, is a town about which almost nothing is known beyond its place on the Harpasus, a tributary of the Maeander. Ptolemy, Stephanus of Byzantium, Hierocles, and Pliny all mention it. Pliny records a rocking stone nearby that a finger could move though a whole body could not.
